Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 27
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Physical Therapist
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Cologne/Perfume): A specific perfume or cologne, Somatic (Pain): Physical pain in a part of the body, Sexual Situations: Sexual situations or intimacy
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociation: I pretend it happened to someone else, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

Vignette:
Karim was twenty-three when it happened—a night that began as routine and fractured into something he has spent the last four years trying to forget, even as his body refuses to let him. He had gone to a nightclub in downtown Boston with colleagues from the rehabilitation clinic where he was doing his clinical internship. The air was thick with cologne and perfume, the kind of sensory saturation he usually found energizing. He remembered the bass thrumming through his chest, the press of bodies on the dance floor, the sense of being young and invulnerable. He remembered a man—someone he thought was friendly, someone who had bought him drinks—guiding him toward a back hallway. He remembered the smell of that man's cologne, something with amber and musk, and then the shock of being shoved into a bathroom stall, the sudden violence of it, hands that were not his own on his body, pain that seemed to split him in half. The specificity of those sensations—the cologne, the cold tile wall against his face, the man's breathing—had never faded. They returned unbidden, visceral and immediate, as though four years were nothing.

When Karim left the bathroom, he told no one. He drove home in silence, showered until his skin was raw, and went to bed as if nothing had happened. For weeks he functioned—he completed his internship, graduated with his DPT, married Yasmin, whom he had been dating since college. But the world had become a place of hidden threats. Certain scents—cologne, perfume, even some of the stronger essential oils his clinic used in the wellness room—would send him into a state of alert so acute that his hands would shake and his heart would race as though the attack were happening again in real time. He found himself unable to be touched unexpectedly. When Yasmin reached for him in the kitchen, or when a patient at the clinic accidentally brushed against him during a treatment, he would flinch violently, his nervous system hijacking his response before his mind could catch up. Beyond these specific triggers, Karim had developed a baseline jumpiness that permeated his days. A car door slamming outside would send electricity through his limbs. The sudden ring of his phone made him gasp. When Yasmin came home from work and unlocked the front door, he would startle at the sound, his body tensing as though bracing for impact. He had taken to keeping the television on at low volume constantly, a white noise that paradoxically made him feel safer by masking the unpredictable sounds of the world. The pain in his body—a chronic tension in his lower back and hips, the very places where he had been hurt—became a constant sentinel, a reminder that his physical form was not entirely his own. He began checking himself obsessively, pressing on his ribs and abdomen, assessing his own body as though it might betray him again. At night, he would lie awake replaying the attack, unable to stop the film reel that played in his mind's eye, seeing the man's face, hearing the sounds, feeling the panic as though it were happening for the first time.

At work, where he spent his days helping patients recover from their own injuries, Karim found himself dissociating during certain moments. When a male patient came in after being assaulted, or when he had to touch someone's lower back, he would mentally step outside himself, imagining that it was someone else in the room, someone else's hands moving across the patient's spine. This dissociation was a relief, a way of making the work survivable. But it was also evidence of something he had come to believe with certainty: that he could no longer trust his own mind or body to protect him. He had misjudged the man at the club entirely—had read friendliness where there was predation, had accepted drinks without considering danger. If his judgment had failed so catastrophically in that moment, how could he trust it now? Every decision felt fraught with the possibility of error. When Yasmin asked him where he wanted to go for dinner, or when a patient asked his professional opinion about their recovery, Karim felt a creeping paralysis. His instincts had already betrayed him once. What if they did so again? He had come to see himself as fundamentally unreliable, a person whose own mind could not be depended upon to keep him safe. The shame was suffocating—shame not just about what had been done to him, but about his body itself, as though it had somehow invited this violation, as though he had somehow been complicit in his own assault through his own stupidity and naïveté.

What had begun as avoidance of specific triggers—he started declining social invitations, making excuses not to go to restaurants or shops where he might encounter strong scents, avoiding the downtown area entirely—had calcified into something larger. Intimacy with Yasmin became impossible. She would initiate sex and he would feel panic rising in his throat, his body rigid, his mind somewhere else entirely. He had come to believe that he would never feel normal again, that something fundamental had been broken in him. By twenty-seven, Karim's life had contracted around these fears. He had stopped going to the clinic's social events. He avoided certain streets where the nightclub was located. He had begun wearing noise-canceling headphones even at home, a barrier between himself and the world. His clinical work, once a source of pride, had become something he endured rather than engaged with, his dissociative episodes occurring with increasing frequency until he found himself questioning whether he was competent enough to be treating patients at all. He had started calling in sick more often, unable to face the sensory landscape of the clinic—the scents of various therapeutic oils, the unpredictability of touch, the vulnerability of being in a room with bodies that were not his own.

Yasmin had grown distant, hurt and confused by his withdrawal. Last month, after she asked him directly whether he was still attracted to her, and he could not answer because the truth was too complicated and too shameful, she suggested that he speak to someone. It was not an ultimatum, but it felt close. Karim finally called a trauma-informed therapist, terrified of what it would mean to put the event into words, but more terrified still of losing the one person who had stayed. What frightened him most as he sat in the waiting room before his first appointment was not the prospect of reliving the trauma itself, but the possibility that once he examined it closely, he would discover that his instincts had been so fundamentally broken that no amount of therapy could repair them—that he truly could not rely on himself ever again.
